subject: physics
question_text: Write the relation between the specific heats of an ideal gas.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 12 Very Short Answer Question 9 (printed p.125; printed wording 'Write the specific heat relation for an ideal gas'). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The two-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: C_P − C_V = R holds for the MOLAR specific heats of an ideal gas, R the universal gas constant; C_P exceeds C_V because a gas heated at constant pressure also does external work as it expands, needing more heat for the same rise in temperature than at constant volume. The per-unit-mass form c_P − c_V = R/M, with M the molar mass, is a DIFFERENT relation and is not what this card states.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.margin_note: First mark. Write C_P − C_V = R and say plainly these are MOLAR specific heats.
steps.why: The per-unit-mass specific heats of the same gas satisfy a different relation, c_P − c_V = R/M, so naming C_P and C_V as molar keeps this relation from being applied to the wrong pair of quantities.
common_mistakes: Writing C_P − C_V = R beside a per-unit-mass specific heat without saying it is molar — the per-mass relation is c_P − c_V = R/M.
Writing C_V − C_P = R with the sign reversed — C_P is the larger of the two.

recall.must_convey: That for an ideal gas the MOLAR specific heats satisfy C_P minus C_V equal to R, the universal gas constant.
accept: C P minus C V equals R
reject: c P minus c V equals R by M

steps.memory_tip: Molar C_P minus molar C_V equals R — the per-mass form divides R by the molar mass M.

steps.margin_note: Second mark. State C_P > C_V and give the reason — the extra work done at constant pressure.
steps.why: The relation C_P − C_V = R only makes physical sense once the extra heat needed at constant pressure is accounted for — stating why C_P is the larger one is what the relation says in words.
common_mistakes: Saying C_V is greater than C_P — at constant pressure the gas does extra work, so C_P is the larger.
Giving no reason and only stating C_P > C_V.

recall.must_convey: That C_P is greater than C_V because at constant pressure the gas also does work as it expands, needing more heat for the same temperature rise.
accept: C P greater than C V
gas does work at constant pressure
more heat needed at constant pressure
reject: C V greater than C P

steps.memory_tip: Constant pressure needs extra heat for the work of expansion, so C_P wins.

insider_note: Say MOLAR explicitly next to C_P − C_V = R — the per-unit-mass relation is c_P − c_V = R/M, a different formula for a different pair of quantities (see vsaq6).
